Laadan
lā´ă-dăn
n. (a Gershonite Levite head; also an ancestor of Joshua)
Hebrew Ladan, of uncertain meaning; the same Levite appears elsewhere as Libni. He heads one of the two Gershonite houses in David's reorganisation of the temple service.

Biblical Definition

One bearer stands in Ephraim's line, three generations above Joshua: “Laadan his son, Ammihud his son, Elishama his son” (1 Chronicles 7:26). The better-known Laadan heads a Levitical house: “Of the Gershonites were, Laadan, and Shimei” (1 Chronicles 23:7), and his own sons are named: “The sons of Laadan; the chief was Jehiel, and Zetham, and Joel, three” (1 Chronicles 23:8). The chapter he belongs to is one of the most consequential administrative acts in the Old Testament. David, old and full of days, numbered the Levites and assigned them by courses, and the reason he gave changed what the tribe would do for the next thousand years: “For David said, The LORD God of Israel hath given rest unto his people, that they may dwell in Jerusalem for ever” (1 Chronicles 23:25). The Levites had existed to carry the tabernacle from place to place. With a permanent house coming, their work was reorganised toward song, gatekeeping, courts and instruction.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) has no entry for Laadan; the name belongs to a head of the Gershonite Levites and to an ancestor of Joshua.

expand to see more

LAADAN, n. A head of the Gershonite Levites in David's reorganisation of the temple service.

GERSHONITES, n. The family of Levites descended from Gershon, the eldest son of Levi.

COURSE, n. Order of succession; a series of appointed turns, as of priests and Levites on duty.

REST, n. Cessation of labor or motion; quiet; repose; the rest promised to the people of God.

REORGANIZE, v.t. To organize anew; to reduce again to a regular body or system.

Modern Corruption

Change in the forms of ministry is resisted as unfaithfulness, or embraced as an end in itself, where Scripture shows a reorganisation made for a stated theological reason.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is how 1 Chronicles 23 reasons about change. The Levites' original charge was portage — bearing the tabernacle, its boards, hangings and vessels, through the wilderness. David reassigns them, and he gives the ground in one sentence: the LORD God of Israel hath given rest unto His people, that they may dwell in Jerusalem for ever. The circumstance God had granted changed, so the shape of the service changed, and the change was made deliberately and on a theological premise rather than from restlessness.

Both modern errors are rebuked by that. The congregation that treats every inherited arrangement as untouchable would have kept four thousand men trained to carry boards for a tent that no longer moved. The congregation that changes for novelty's sake has no premise at all; David had one, and it was about what God had done. The Reformed rule holds the line between them: the elements of worship are fixed by Scripture and not open to invention, while the circumstances — hours, order, arrangement, division of labour — are to be ordered by the light of nature and Christian prudence. Laadan's house is what that looks like in practice.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Ladan (H3936), Laadan; Gereshon (H1648), Gershon; machaloqoth (H4256), courses; nuach (H5117), to give rest.

expand to see more

Hebrew Ladan (H3936) — Laadan; a Gershonite head, elsewhere called Libni.

Hebrew Gereshon (H1648) — Gershon, eldest son of Levi.

Hebrew machaloqoth (H4256) — courses, divisions; the Levites assigned by turns.

Hebrew nuach (H5117) — to rest, give rest; hath given rest unto his people.

Hebrew abodah (H5656) — service, labour; the work of the house of the LORD.

Usage

"“Of the Gershonites were, Laadan, and Shimei” — the two houses."

"“The sons of Laadan; the chief was Jehiel” — his own line."

"“The LORD God of Israel hath given rest unto his people” — the reason for the change."
